examples.text: Самые неукротимые хунны сбежали от врага далеко на запад, в Приуралье, и осели там среди местных жителей из угорской языковой семьи.

glosses: To hit someone with a car or other vehicle and injure or kill them.

examples.text: He was run down while crossing the main road.

glosses: To criticize someone or an organisation, often unfairly.

examples.text: Whatever the company says, the media is going to run them down.
My sister is always running me down in front of my friends.
Don't run yourself down so much!
Ha! ha! ha! 'tis very hard for them to leave a subject they have not quite run down.

Since I have put my name in GCN and received my first paper, I have only received two letters. But the one that pissed me off […] was from Bible belt hypocrite. He sent me an envelope full of tracts about homosexuality. Well, I have this to say to whoever he is (The person that's got nothing better to do than get the GCN to see who he can run down should take a damn good look at himself).

glosses: To find something or someone after searching for a long time.

examples.text: I finally managed to run down that report. I had filed it incorrectly.

glosses: To lose power slowly. Used for a machine, battery, or other powered device.

examples.text: You need to wind up the clock every day so that it doesn't run down.
If you don't switch off the car lights, you will run the battery down.

glosses: To read quickly a list or other short text.

examples.text: Running down the list of suggestions, I can see three we can discard immediately.

glosses: To describe in the form of a rundown, a rough outline or summary.

examples.text: When the minute was up, John Jay managed to make the woman twice as nervous as he ran down the rules and the possibilities.

glosses: To reduce the size or stock levels of a business, often with a view to closure.

examples.text: The board of directors have decided to run down the stocks held in storage prior to offering the company for sale.
Social media has been full of strident criticism of a Government perceived as pursuing a conscious policy to run down - even destroy - our railway.

glosses: To decline in quality or condition.

examples.text: to run down in health

TravelWatch SouthWest Chairman Chris Irwin said: "This is intolerable. The South West deserves levelling up, not running down. SWR and its sponsors in the Department of Transport must be called to account."

glosses: To chase till the object pursued is captured or exhausted.

examples.text: to run down a stag

glosses: To run against and sink, as a vessel.

examples.text: The Jylland only missed running down a schooner by a few yards in the fog; it was a near thing—near enough, in fact, to allow of some shouted remarks between those on the bridge of the motorship and the man at the wheel of the schooner to be clearly heard.
Hiei now loomed into the action, causing the leading U.S. destroyers to scatter before the oncoming behemoth lest they be run down.

glosses: To crush; to overthrow; to overbear.

examples.text: Religion is […]run down by the prevailing licence of these times.

glosses: To approach (someone, thing or place) aggressively, as to attack.

examples.text: He ran down on Rashad and them.

glosses: To move (some copy) down to the next line.

examples.text: If they occasionally supply any additional copy after this element, run it down with a manual line break.

examples.text: The crowd had to run away from the burning structure with only the clothes on their backs.

glosses: To leave home, or other place of residence, usually unannounced, or to make good on a threat, with such action usually performed by a child or juvenile.

examples.text: My parents want me to take a bath every day? Fine, I'm running away.

glosses: To become a runaway. (of a device or vehicle)

examples.text: The complete 1892 rebuilding, indeed, followed an accident in 1890, when No. 6 ran away down the Buckley branch, and got badly smashed up in a collision at Connah's Quay.
The train's brakes failed and it ran away.
An autotrim failure can cause stabiliser trim to rapidly run away in the nose-up or nose-down direction.

glosses: To get free; to free oneself.

examples.text: The prisoners escaped by jumping over a wall.
The factory was evacuated after toxic gases escaped from a pipe.

glosses: To avoid (any unpleasant person or thing); to elude, get away from.

examples.text: The children climbed out of the window to escape the fire.
He only got a fine and so escaped going to jail.
sailors that escaped the wreck

Luiz was Chelsea's stand-out performer, although Ferguson also had a case when he questioned how the £21m defender escaped a red card after the break for a hack at Rooney, with the Brazilian having already been booked.

glosses: To avoid capture; to get away with something, avoid punishment.

examples.text: Luckily, I escaped with only a fine.

glosses: To elude the observation or notice of; to not be seen or remembered by.

examples.text: The name of the hotel escapes me at present.
